title: Interacting galaxies Arp 142 (NIRCam and MIRI image)
caption: The interacting galaxies Arp 142, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
celestial: Arp 142 · constellation Hydra · about 326 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #63 on ESA/Webb’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A distorted spiral nicknamed the Penguin and a compact oval galaxy called the Egg sit side by side, joined by a faint, upside-down U-shaped blue glow. Together they are Arp 142, about 326 million light-years away in Hydra, seen here in near- and mid-infrared light in a Webb image made to mark its second year of science.

The pair first swept past each other between 25 and 75 million years ago. That encounter unwound the Penguin's coiled arms, threw gas and dust in many directions and set off a wave of new stars, about 100 to 200 per year; the Milky Way, by comparison, makes roughly six to seven. Today the Penguin's centre resembles an eye, with star trails shaped like a beak, a backbone and a fanned tail.
Although the Penguin looks far bigger, the two have about the same mass, one reason they have not merged yet. The Egg holds old stars and little gas or dust, so it keeps its compact shape.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.23 x 3.11 arcminutes) and distance (326 million light years), the frame spans roughly 211,000 × 295,000 light-years. Its light set out about 326 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI combined near- and mid-infrared light: blue and green show the shortest wavelengths, yellow and orange longer near-infrared light plus a mid-infrared PAH dust filter, and red a mix of the longest near-infrared filter and mid-infrared filters, including one for silicate dust.
understand.eye: Almost all of this light is infrared, which the human eye cannot see.

explore: The bright edge-on galaxy at top right, PGC 1237172, is not part of the encounter: it lies 100 million light-years closer to us. It is young and not very dusty, so it nearly vanishes in Webb's mid-infrared view. Stars rarely collide when galaxies interact, but their orbits get disrupted. The Egg's stars are packed so tightly that it shows four diffraction spikes.
alt: Two interacting galaxies: a compact oval galaxy on the left and a distorted spiral on the right whose beak-like region points toward it, linked by a faint blue U-shaped glow, with many distant galaxies behind.
